v.why: Stacked layers compound large Adam steps into divergence or dead ReLUs, so adding depth hurts more at high learning rates.
Noisy tiny-batch gradients are amplified through more layers, making deeper nets harder to train.
Wider layers produce larger aggregate function change per Adam step, compensating for slow learning rates within 243 epochs.
Large batches give few updates, and extra width speeds fitting per update.
sklearn divides the L2 penalty by batch size, so tiny batches inflate the effective penalty and over-regularize.
Narrow nets have little spare capacity, so extra shrinkage causes underfitting.
Small batches already add gradient noise and many updates, so larger steps tip training into instability.
A single hidden layer tolerates large Adam steps without compounding, so it benefits from faster learning.
Larger batches reduce gradient noise, which partially tames the instability of high learning rates.
Larger batches weaken the per-batch-normalized L2 penalty, relieving over-regularization at high alpha.
